description: A smartphone joins a mobile telephone, a general-purpose pocket computer and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, using cellular data to reach the internet wherever coverage exists. Handheld devices combining phones and personal organisers appeared in the 1990s, such as IBM's Simon (1994). Touchscreen models from 2007 onward, including Apple's iPhone and Android phones, spread the form worldwide within about a decade.
uncertainty: What counts as the 'first' smartphone depends on definition (IBM Simon, Nokia Communicator, BlackBerry, iPhone); adoption pace varied widely by country.

description: Cyber operations use computer networks to spy on, disrupt or damage an opponent's systems, while defenders rely on encryption, authentication, monitoring and prompt repair of software flaws. Stuxnet, malicious code publicly identified in 2010, sabotaged uranium-enrichment centrifuges at Iran's Natanz plant. It is often called the first known code built to cause physical destruction; no government has officially acknowledged responsibility.
uncertainty: Attribution of Stuxnet (widely reported as a United States-Israeli operation) is unofficial; whether it was the first physically destructive cyber attack depends on what earlier incidents are counted.

description: A quantum computer stores information in qubits, which can hold superpositions and become entangled, so some calculations proceed in ways ordinary computers cannot efficiently imitate. Richard Feynman argued in 1981-82 that they could simulate physics. In 2019 Google's 53-qubit Sycamore processor ran a narrow sampling task claimed to be beyond classical reach, a claim IBM disputed. Early machines remain noisy.
uncertainty: The 2019 'quantum supremacy' claim was disputed (IBM estimated a classical simulation in days) and later classical algorithms narrowed the gap; several groups and approaches (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic) contributed to early quantum computing.

description: Numerical weather prediction forecasts the atmosphere by solving equations for motion, heat and moisture on a grid, starting from conditions reported by stations and radio balloons. Lewis Fry Richardson hand-computed a forecast during the First World War; published in 1922, it failed badly. In 1950 a Princeton team including Jule Charney produced the first successful computer forecasts, on ENIAC.
uncertainty: Operational routine forecasting began in the mid-1950s (Sweden and the United States are both cited); the 1950 ENIAC runs used a simplified one-layer model and took about as long as the weather they forecast.

description: Fault-tolerant quantum computing is a goal rather than an achieved technology: machines correcting their own errors faster than errors arise, keeping long calculations reliable. Quantum error-correcting codes, first proposed by Peter Shor in 1995, spread one robust logical qubit across many fragile physical ones. If built at scale, such machines could simulate molecules and materials beyond practical classical reach.
uncertainty: Speculative: no large fault-tolerant machine exists; timelines, the best qubit technology and the size of the practical advantage for chemistry are all contested.

description: General machine intelligence means hypothetical computer systems able to learn and perform most intellectual tasks people can, not one narrow job. uncertainty: Speculative and definition-dependent: there is no agreed test for general intelligence, and expert forecasts of if and when it could exist differ widely.

description: Space-based solar power is a proposed system in which large satellites collect sunlight in high orbit, above clouds and in near-continuous daylight, and beam the energy to ground receivers as microwaves or laser light. Peter Glaser described such a design in 1968. Small power-beaming tests have flown, but launch and assembly costs have so far prevented any working power station.
uncertainty: Speculative: no operational plant exists; cost, efficiency of beaming, and safety and spectrum issues are unresolved, and national programmes have repeatedly been studied and shelved.

description: Energy-conversion research seeks more useful work per unit of fuel or sunlight. Physics sets ceilings: Sadi Carnot's 1824 analysis bounds any heat engine's efficiency by its operating temperatures, and William Shockley and Hans-Joachim Queisser calculated in 1961 that a single-junction solar cell cannot convert much more than about a third of sunlight. Combined-cycle plants and multi-junction cells show continuing gains.

claims: Carnot gave the first successful theory of the maximum efficiency of heat engines

uncertainty: Practical limits sit well below the theoretical ceilings and depend on materials, cost and operating conditions; the precise single-junction limit varies with assumptions (about 30-34 percent).

description: Computation research seeks more calculation per unit of energy, material and labour. For decades transistor counts on chips doubled roughly every two years, a trend Gordon Moore described in 1965 and revised in 1975; the pace has since slowed. Rolf Landauer argued in 1961 that erasing one bit must release a minimum of heat, a floor far below present chips.
uncertainty: The end or slowing of Moore's law is dated differently by different analysts; how closely practical computing can approach the Landauer limit is an open research question.

description: The first programmable digital computers performed long calculations automatically, following instructions set by punched tape, switches or plugboard wiring rather than held in memory. They arose largely independently: Konrad Zuse's relay-based Z3 ran in Berlin in 1941; valve-based Colossus machines attacked German teleprinter ciphers at Bletchley Park from 1944; and ENIAC, completed in Philadelphia in 1945-46, computed artillery tables.
uncertainty: Which machine was 'first' depends on criteria (programmable, electronic, general-purpose, Turing-complete); Colossus was special-purpose, and the first Colossus ran in December 1943 or January 1944. ENIAC's completion is dated 1945 or 1946 in different sources. Stibitz's relay calculators at Bell Labs are a further independent strand.

description: Semiconductor physics explains why materials like silicon and germanium conduct electricity better than insulators but worse than metals. In 1931 Alan Wilson used quantum mechanics to describe their energy bands; Walter Schottky and Nevill Mott explained rectifying metal contacts in 1938-39, clarifying radio crystal detectors. In 1940 Russell Ohl at Bell Labs found a silicon junction generating voltage under light.
uncertainty: Band theory was built by several physicists (Bloch, Peierls, Wilson and others); Schottky and Mott (and Davydov) worked on rectification largely independently; Ohl's junction is dated 1940 or about 1941, a priority claim for Vadym Lashkaryov has been argued, and the p-n junction was understood only gradually.
